meta.titre: Thermometers and temperature scales: matching the instrument and converting readings
meta.sous_theme: types of thermometer and scale conversion

sections.contenu_markdown: In a pharmacy in Douala you can buy a glass thermometer for your fever, while a technician at a power station uses a probe connected to a meter to check the temperature of a transformer, and a laboratory uses a digital instrument for ice baths. These instruments look nothing alike, yet they all turn a changing physical property into a temperature number. GCE questions combine the two ideas of this topic: which thermometer suits the job, and how a raw reading is converted into degrees Celsius and kelvin.

items: A thermometric property is a property that changes steadily with temperature.
The Celsius scale uses melting ice at $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and steam at standard pressure at $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.
The kelvin scale is obtained by adding 273 to the Celsius temperature.

sections.titre: One conversion method for every thermometer, and how to choose
sections.contenu_markdown:
**One method for every thermometer.** Whatever property $X$ a thermometer uses, we read $X$ at the two fixed points and then assume it changes uniformly:

$$\theta=\frac{X_\theta-X_0}{X_{100}-X_0}\times100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\qquad\qquad T=\theta+273\ \ (\mathrm{K})$$

$X$ can be the length of a thread (mm), the resistance of a wire ($\Omega$), the e.m.f. of a thermocouple (mV) or the pressure of a gas (kPa). Only the property changes; the formula does not.

**Comparing thermometers.**

| Thermometer | Property | Typical range | Main advantage | Main disadvantage |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mercury-in-glass | thread length | $-39$ to $357\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ | simple, accurate, no power needed | fragile, cannot read very low temperatures |
| Alcohol-in-glass | thread length | $-115$ to $78\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ | measures very low temperatures | cannot measure boiling water |
| Clinical | thread length | $35$ to $42\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ | very sensitive, keeps its reading | tiny range |
| Resistance | resistance | very wide | can be read at a distance | needs a meter and a power supply |
| Thermocouple | e.m.f. | very wide, very hot places | very small probe, fast response | needs a sensitive voltmeter |

**Choosing a thermometer.** Look at four things: the **range** needed, the **sensitivity** required, how **fast** it must respond, and whether it must be **read remotely** or kept as a record. A clinical thermometer is chosen for sensitivity, a thermocouple for a hot furnace, alcohol for a very cold freezer.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked why two different thermometers give slightly different readings between the fixed points.
variantes.contenu_markdown: All thermometers are made to agree at the two fixed points because that is how they are calibrated. Between those points different liquids and different properties do not change in exactly the same way with temperature, so two thermometers can show slightly different values, for example $52\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $53\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, at the same place. The assumption of uniform change is a good approximation, not an exact law.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question asks you to name a modern alternative to mercury.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Digital thermometers use a small **thermistor** or resistance sensor and a circuit which converts the resistance into a number on a display. They avoid mercury (which is poisonous), respond quickly and are used in homes and clinics, but they need a battery.

sections.enonce_markdown:
A resistance thermometer has a resistance of $50\ \Omega$ in pure melting ice and $70\ \Omega$ in steam at standard pressure. It is placed in a tank of hot water used in a dye factory and its resistance is $62\ \Omega$.

(a) State the thermometric property used.

(b) Calculate the temperature of the water in degrees Celsius and in kelvin.

etapes.action: Name the property and list the readings.
etapes.justification: The thermometer works by the change of the resistance of its wire with temperature.

etapes.action: Find the fundamental interval in resistance.
etapes.justification: It is the change of resistance between the two fixed points.

etapes.action: Find the change of resistance from the ice point.
etapes.justification: Only the rise above $R_0$ is caused by the temperature.
Assume uniform change of resistance with temperature.

sections.conclusion_markdown: **(a)** The electrical resistance of the wire. **(b)** The water is at **$60\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$**, that is **$333\ \mathrm{K}$**.

items.pourquoi_faux: The resistance at $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ is not zero. Dividing the raw reading by the upper-point reading ignores the starting value $R_0$.

items.erreur_markdown: “All thermometers must read exactly the same temperature everywhere between the fixed points.”
items.pourquoi_faux: They only agree at the fixed points used for calibration. Different liquids and properties change slightly differently in between.
items.correction_markdown: They agree at $0$ and $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and give close but not always identical readings between these points.

items.erreur_markdown: “A clinical thermometer is a good choice for measuring the temperature of boiling palm oil.”
items.pourquoi_faux: Its range stops at about $42\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, so the mercury would burst out of the stem and the thermometer would break.
items.correction_markdown: Use a laboratory mercury thermometer (up to about $110\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ or more) or a thermocouple for such high temperatures.

items.erreur_markdown: A student finds $\theta=45\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and writes the answer in kelvin as $45\ \mathrm{K}$.
items.pourquoi_faux: The kelvin scale starts at absolute zero, $-273\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, so a Celsius temperature is not equal to the same number of kelvin.

items.enonce_markdown:
Choose the most suitable thermometer for each job and give one reason.

(a) measuring the body temperature of a child

(b) checking a freezer kept near $-60\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$

(c) measuring the temperature inside a brick kiln at over $800\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$

Choose from: clinical thermometer, alcohol-in-glass thermometer, thermocouple.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) **Clinical thermometer**: its narrow range makes it very sensitive and it keeps the reading.

(b) **Alcohol-in-glass thermometer**: alcohol stays liquid down to $-115\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, whereas mercury would freeze at $-39\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

(c) **Thermocouple**: it can work at very high temperatures where glass thermometers would melt or break, and its probe is small and responds quickly.

items.enonce_markdown: The pressure of the gas in a constant-volume gas thermometer is $80\ \mathrm{kPa}$ at the lower fixed point and $110\ \mathrm{kPa}$ at the upper fixed point. When it is placed in a cup of tea the pressure is $92\ \mathrm{kPa}$. Find the temperature of the tea in $^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and in $\mathrm{K}$.

Thermometer A is a liquid-in-glass thermometer whose thread is $30\ \mathrm{mm}$ long in melting ice and $130\ \mathrm{mm}$ long in steam. Thermometer B is a resistance thermometer with $40\ \Omega$ at the lower fixed point and $60\ \Omega$ at the upper fixed point. Both are put in the same bath and A shows a thread length of $75\ \mathrm{mm}$.

(a) Find the temperature of the bath in $^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and in $\mathrm{K}$.

(b) What resistance should B show?

(c) The bath cools by $12\ \mathrm{K}$. What is the new temperature in $^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and what is the new resistance of B?
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $\theta=\dfrac{75-30}{130-30}\times100=\dfrac{45}{100}\times100=$ **$45\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$**, and $T=45+273=$ **$318\ \mathrm{K}$**.

(b) The resistance rises $20\ \Omega$ over $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, i.e. $0.20\ \Omega$ per degree. $R=40+0.20\times45=$ **$49\ \Omega$**.

(c) A fall of $12\ \mathrm{K}$ is a fall of $12\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, so the new temperature is $45-12=$ **$33\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$**. Then $R=40+0.20\times33=$ **$46.6\ \Omega$**.

items_markdown: For any thermometer: $\theta=\dfrac{X_\theta-X_0}{X_{100}-X_0}\times100$, where $X$ is the thermometric property; then $T=\theta+273$.
Mercury suits high temperatures, alcohol very low ones, the clinical thermometer suits fever readings, a thermocouple suits very hot places.
Choose a thermometer by range, sensitivity, speed of response and whether it can be read remotely.
Different thermometers agree at the fixed points but may differ slightly between them.
A temperature change is the same number in K and in degrees Celsius; a temperature reading is not.
